tokens.en: The boy's name was Santiago.
The boy's name was Santiago; dusk was falling as he arrived with his herd of sheep at an abandoned church.
Its roof had long since collapsed, and a huge sycamore tree was growing on the spot where the sacristy once stood.
He decided to spend the night there.
He saw his sheep going in through the broken gate, then placed a board over the broken gate so the herd would not wander off in the night.
There were no wolves in this area, but a sheep had once gotten lost in the night, and the boy had to search for it the whole next day.
He swept the floor with his jacket and lay down, using the book he had just finished reading as a pillow.
He said to himself that he should start reading thicker books: they last longer and make more comfortable pillows.
It was still dark when he woke up, and tilting his head back, he could see the stars through the half-destroyed roof.
I want to sleep a little longer, he thought.
He had the same dream he'd had a week ago, and once again he woke up before the dream finished.
He got up, took his staff, and woke the sheep that were still sleeping.
He noticed that, as soon as he awoke, most of his animals also began to stir.
It seemed there was some mysterious energy connecting his life with those of the sheep, who had been with him for two years, leading them through the countryside in search of food and water.
"They have become so used to me that they know my schedule,"
he murmured.
Thinking about this for a moment, he realized it could be the other way around: it was he who had become used to their schedule.
But some were harder to wake.
The boy poked them, one by one, with his staff, calling each by name.
He believed the sheep could understand what he said.
So sometimes he would read them passages from his book that had made an impression on him, or tell them about the loneliness and happiness of a shepherd in the fields.
Occasionally he commented to them about what he had seen in the villages they passed through.
But in the last few days, he had spoken to his sheep about only one thing: the girl, the daughter of a merchant who lived in the village they would reach in about four days.
He had only been to that village once, the previous year.
The merchant was the owner of a fabric shop, and he always insisted that the sheep be sheared in front of him so he wouldn't be cheated.
A friend had told the boy about the fabric shop, and so he brought his sheep there.
"I want to sell wool," the boy said to the merchant.
The shop was busy, so the merchant told the shepherd to wait until evening.
So the boy sat down on the steps of the shop and took a book out of his bag.
"So there are shepherds who can read too," came the voice of a girl behind him.
The girl's face was typical of the Andalusia region, with wavy black hair and eyes that vaguely recalled the Moorish conquerors.
"Well... usually I learn more from my sheep than from books," he answered.
For two hours they chatted; the girl told him she was the fabric merchant's daughter, and spoke about life in the village, where every day was the same as every other.
The shepherd told the girl about the Andalusian countryside, and other interesting things from the towns he had visited.
A pleasant change from talking to his sheep.
"How did you learn to read?" the girl asked at one point.
"Like everyone else," he said.
"At school."
"Well, if you can read, why are you just a shepherd?"
The boy made an excuse to avoid answering her question.
He was sure the girl would never understand.
He went on telling stories of his travels, and her bright Moorish eyes opened and closed in wonder and surprise.
As time passed, the boy found himself wishing the day would never end, that her father would stay busy and keep him waiting for three days.
He realized he was feeling something he had never felt before: the desire to live in one place forever.
With the girl with the raven hair, his days would never be the same.
But finally the merchant came out and asked him to shear four sheep.
He paid him for the wool and asked him to come back next year.
AND NOW IT WAS ONLY FOUR DAYS BEFORE he would be back at that same village.
He was excited, and at the same time uneasy: perhaps the girl had already forgotten him.
Many shepherds passed through there selling wool.
"It doesn't matter," he said to his sheep.
"I know other girls in other places too."
But in his heart he knew it did matter.
And he knew that shepherds, like sailors and travelling salesmen, always found a town where someone could make them forget the joy of carefree living.
Dawn was breaking, and the shepherd led the sheep out into the sun.
They never have to make decisions, he thought.
Maybe that is why they always stay close to me.
The only things that concerned the sheep were food and water.
As long as the boy knew where to find the best pastures in Andalusia, they would be his friends.

Yes, their days were all the same, with the long hours between sunrise and sunset; and they had never read a single book in their lives, and didn't understand when the boy told them about the new things he had seen in the cities.
They were content with just food and water, and that was enough.
In exchange, they generously gave him their wool, their company, and—occasionally—their meat.
If I were a monster and decided to kill them one by one, they would only realize it after most of the herd had been slaughtered, the boy thought.
They trust me, and they have forgotten how to rely on their own instincts, because I lead them to food.
The boy was surprised by his own thoughts.
Maybe the church, with the sycamore tree growing inside it, was haunted.
That was what had made him dream the same dream twice, and made him feel angry with his faithful companions.
He drank a little of the wine left over from last night's meal, and pulled his jacket tightly around him.
He knew that a few hours from now, with the sun at its peak, the heat would be so intense that he would not be able to lead the sheep across the fields.
It was the time when all of Spain slept during the summer.
The terrible heat continued until evening came, so all through that time he had to carry his jacket with him.
But whenever he wanted to complain about the burden of the jacket, he remembered that because he had the jacket, he could withstand the cold of morning.
We must be ready to face change, he thought, and he was grateful for the thickness of his jacket and its warmth.
The jacket had a purpose, and so did the boy.
His purpose in life was to travel, and, after two years of wandering through Andalusia, he knew every city in the region.
He planned, on this visit, to explain to the girl how a simple shepherd could read.
That he had studied at the seminary until age sixteen.
His parents had wanted him to become a priest, and thereby a source of pride for a poor farming family.
They worked hard just to get food and water, like the sheep.
He had studied Latin, Spanish, and theology.
But since childhood he had wanted to know the world, and this was far more important to him than knowing God and studying the sins of man.
One evening, while visiting his family, he gathered the courage to tell his father that he didn't want to become a priest. That he wanted to wander.
"PEOPLE FROM ALL OVER THE WORLD HAVE PASSED THROUGH this village, Son," said his father.
"They come looking for new things, but when they leave they are basically the same as when they came.
They climb the mountain to see the castle, and they end up concluding that the past was better than the present.
They have blond hair, or dark skin, but basically they are the same as the people who live here."
"But I want to see the castles in the cities where they live," the boy explained.
"Those people, when they see our country, also say they want to live here forever," his father continued.
"Then I want to see their country and see how they live," said the son.
"Those people who come here have lots of money, so they can afford to travel," said his father.
"Among us, only shepherds travel."
"Then I want to be a shepherd!"
His father said nothing more.
The next day, he gave his son a pouch containing three old Spanish gold coins.
"I found these in the field one day. I wanted them to be part of your inheritance.
But use them to buy sheep. Take them to the pastures, and one day you will learn that our villages are the best, and our women are the most beautiful."
And he gave his blessing to his son.

The boy could see in his father's gaze a desire to be able, for himself, to travel around the whole world—a desire still burning, even though his father had tried to bury it, over the years, beneath the burden of struggling for water to drink, food to eat, and the same place to sleep every night of his life.
THE HORIZON BURST INTO COLOR, and suddenly the sun appeared.
The boy reflected on his conversation with his father, and felt happy; he had already seen many castles and met many women (but none equal to the one waiting for him a few days from now).
He had a jacket, a book that could be traded for another, and a herd of sheep.
But, most importantly, every day he could live his dream.
If he grew bored of the fields of Andalusia, he could sell his sheep and go to the sea.
By the time he had grown tired of the sea, he would have known other cities, other women, and other chances that would make him happy.
I cannot find God in the seminary, he thought, as he watched the rising sun.
Whenever he wanted, he found new ways to travel.
He had never been to the place of the ruined church before, though he had often walked through those areas.
The world is so vast and without limits; he allowed his sheep to set the route for just a moment, so that he might find other interesting things.
The problem was that the herd was not even aware they were walking new paths every day.
They did not see that the fields were new and the seasons were changing.
All they thought about was food and water.
Maybe we are all like that, thought the boy.
Even me—I haven't thought about another woman since meeting the merchant's daughter.
Looking toward the sun, he calculated that he would arrive in Tarifa before midday.

There he could exchange his book for a thicker one, refill his wine bottle, shave and cut his hair; he had to prepare himself for the meeting with the girl, and he did not want to think about the possibility that there might be...
